items.title: 아빠와 운전 연습하다가…20대女 몰던 차 미용실 돌진
items.summary: 경남 창원에서 운전 연습을 하던 20대 여성이 몰던 승용차가 아파트 상가 미용실로 돌진해 안에 있던 여성 3명이 다쳤다.14일 창원소방본부와 마산동부경찰서에 따르면 이날 오후 2시 28분경 창원시 마산회원구 내서읍 삼계리의 한 아파트 상가 1층 미용실로 아반떼 승용차가 돌진했다.이 사고로 미용실 업주와 손님 등 50대 여성 3명이 다쳐 병원으로 옮겨졌다. 이들은 경상을 입은 것으로 알려졌다. 미용실 유리창과 내부 집기도 파손됐다.경찰 조사 결과 운전자는 최근 운전면허를 취득한 20대 여성으로, 사고 당시 아버지와 함께 운전 연습을 하던 중이었다. 운전자는 아파트 주차장으로 진입하다 주차된 차량을 피하려는 과정에서 가속 페달을 잘못 밟아 상가로 돌진한 것으로 파악됐다. 음주나 무면허, 약물 운전 상태는 아니었던 것으로 조사됐다.경찰은 정확한 사고 경위를 조사하고 있다.

items.summary: 같은 회사에 근무하는 친고모와 갈등을 빚자 부하직원을 통해 청부 폭행을 의뢰한 30대 조카가 1심에서 징역형의 집행유예를 선고받았다.15일 법조계에 따르면 의정부지법 형사6단독 이용희 판사는 상해교사 혐의로 구속 기소된 30대 남성 A씨에게 징역 2년에 집행유예 3년을 선고했다.범행에 가담해 A씨와 같은 혐의로 기소된 부하직원과 중간 연결책 등 2명에게도 각각 징역 1년 6개월에 집행유예 3년, 징역 10개월에 집행유예 2년을 각각 선고했다.판결문에 따르면 A씨는 회사 자금을 횡령한 사실이 발각되면서 친고모이자 같은 회사에 근무하는 60대 여성 B씨와 갈등을 겪어왔다.이에 앙심을 품은 A씨는 B씨에게 상해를 가해 2~3개월 출근하지 못하게 하겠다고 마음먹고, 부하직원인 C씨에게 “때려주는 애들을 알아보라”고 지시했다.C씨는 지인이자 중간 연결책 역할을 한 D씨와 함께 B씨를 실제로 폭행할 실행자들을 모집했다.이 과정에서 A씨는 실행자들중 한명을 만나 “강하게 부탁한다, 세

items.title: “공항 라운지가 안방인가”…신발 벗고 소파에 다리 쭉 뻗은 가족

items.title: 아파트에 불 질러 14명 사상케 한 40대 구속…법원 “도주 우려”

items.title: 조폐공사 상품권 플랫폼 ‘착’도 뚫렸다…3083명 정보 유출

items.title: The OpenAI board member who fired Sam Altman says we still cant trust AI CEOs
items.summary: Today, I’m talking with Helen Toner, the executive director of the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University. This episode is part two of our series on AI in real life. Helen is a well-known figure in the AI safety and policy community, though she is perhaps best known for having served on the board of OpenAI, when she was one of four board members who voted to fire Sam Altman. That incident, now sometimes referred to as “the blip,” ended with Sam coming back as CEO, Helen resigning, and a new board of directors. OpenAI has since restructured entirely. But it’s worth remembering what Helen and the board were supposed to do: OpenAI’s nonprofit board existed specifically to make sure the company didn’t betray its mission to build safe AI by prioritizing profit and growth over safety. When the board actually tried to pull the lever, that accountability mechanism broke, and here we are. Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here. Now, the question of AI safety is everywhere. This summer, AI models from OpenAI and Anthropic broke out of their testing environments and hacked real companies. The CEOs of these frontier labs have since called for a slowdown and asked Washington for help, but the White House’s answer was a voluntary accord — one that relies in part on the kind of board accountability that failed at OpenAI. Anthropic is also about to go public, which will put a whole new set of market pressures on OpenAI’s biggest competitor. Helen has seen up close what happens when safety commitments run headlong into commercial incentives. And as she put it to me, if our hopes for the future depend on any one person being trustworthy, we’re in big trouble. So we talked about what we might do instead: what the labs are actually trying to build, whether AI alignment is a problem that can be solved, and what a smarter approach to AI regulation might look like. That includes how to think about China, which is the issue that looms large in every policy conversation about AI right now — especially now after the Jensen Huang affair. Just for clarity, Helen and I talked before Nvidia opened its investigation and Jensen ultimately resigned, so you won’t hear us talk about that directly. Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday. Okay: Helen Toner, the executive director of CSET, on the future of AI safety. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Helen Toner, you’re the executive director for the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University. Welcome to Decoder. Thanks so much. Great to be here. I have wanted to talk to you for 10 million years. I am so excited you’re here. You’ve been involved in a lot of AI safety and ethics ideas for a long time. You were obviously on the board of OpenAI during what everyone has come to call “the blip.” Now, you’re talking a lot about AI safety, about which I have 10 million questions. But let’s just start at the start. You run the Center for Security and Emerging Technology, people call it CSET. What is CSET? It’s awesome to be here. I’m really excited to talk to you as well. CSET is a team inside Georgetown, but we’re really not academics. We’re about 50 people and have been going since 2019. Basically in 2019, a group of us decided that there was a lot happening and a lot of emerging technologies that were becoming very relevant in the national security space, and the security space more broadly,. And some policymakers who had very important jobs did not have the time or the expertise to get across what was going on with those emerging technologies. Already at the top of our list in 2019 was AI. Basically our mission is to do analysis that is really rigorous, but also actionable, for policymakers and analysis that is both grounded in the technology and grounded in real national security expertise and understanding and issues. We produce long reports. We go do short briefings on those long reports to busy policymakers. We have a big data team that helps us do our research. We do all kinds of cool stuff. Can I just ask about the dynamics of that for one minute? You and I are talking the day after the midterm elections in the United States of America, and there was a big blue wave. There’s a lot of polling that says the number one issue is corruption. We’re going to throw the bums out. We’re going to start over and get rid of these corrupt guys. The AI industry, and the tech industry, has flooded a bunch of money into politics. And then somewhere next to that is, “Oh, there’s a bunch of well-meaning researchers who are going to show up and tell you how it actually works and what the real risks are.” It just occurs to me that maybe people don’t believe that’s effective anymore, that the money and the corruption and the AI CEO standing next to Trump have completely outweighed the well-meaning, sincere, “here are the actual problems” research that you do. What is that dynamic actually like? It’s a reasonable concern to have, and there are definitely some spaces where money just absolutely overwhelms everything. I’m Australian. I didn’t grow up in the US, and so the amount of money in US elections is pretty mind-blowing to me, but there are limits to what money can do. AI is a great example. In this election, there were just unbelievable amounts of money being thrown at candidates, at messages, at opposition research. There was all kinds of astroturfing on Twitter, and some very strange things trying to get anyone who talked about AI governance, regulation, safety, any of those words thrown out or not elected. It turns out to have really not worked very well. I think the reason that it didn’t work very well is one, this is an issue that voters increasingly care about. And two, also interestingly, it’s an issue that is pretty bipartisan at this point. What we see in our work is that there is a real thirst among policymakers for high-quality information. That’s members of Congress for sure, but they’re also in the executive branch, just a lot of people who have these very busy jobs and are seeing AI playing a larger and larger role in their work and their world. In DC, if you live and work here, you know that lobbyists in DC are not just people who go in and push their company’s position, though they do do that. They’re also educators. A big reason that congressional staff and others want to have lobbyists come talk to them is because they’ll really help them understand the weeds of a given piece of legislation — what does it mean for that industry and so on and so forth. What we find over and over again is we can go in and say, “Hey, we are independent. We’re nonpartisan. We do really rigorous work. We’re just here to help and we can go into the weeds with you as well.” There’s a ton of interest in that and appetite for that. It’s been really encouraging over the past seven to eight years. Are you doing that with the principals, the members of Congress, or are you doing that with the staff? Everyone and anyone. Again, we do a good amount of work with Congress on Capitol Hill, with some members of Congress, with lots of staff. We do hearings and briefings. Also, we do lots in the executive branch, with different agencies — the White House, Department of War, Department of State, Department of Commerce, all across the board at different levels, depending on the topic and what’s happening at any given moment. The reason I’m starting here is I want to have a pretty heady conversation with you, but I know what our audience thinks and it’s just that the government doesn’t get it. There’s no way the government will ever catch up to the tech industry. There’s no way they’ll ever write a regulation. They should just get out of the way. In this election cycle, I’ve seen a number of candidate forum videos where someone was like, “I’ve tried Claude once.” There’s some huge gap, real or perceived. I’m just trying to understand how you see that gap, how big you think that gap is, because as we get into AI safety and regulation, it’s that gap that has to close. There absolutely is a gap. It absolutely is a big gap. It also is possible to overestimate the gap from outside, or if you’re just looking across from California. I lived in the Bay Area for three years, so I definitely am very familiar with this perspective. I know a lot of people from the tech industry who come over and start talking to congressional staff or staffers in executive branch offices. Once they actually start having those conversations, they’re like, “Wow, these people are really smart. The staff do actually know what they’re talking about.” With principals, it is a different issue. Some of them are in the older generations, but they’re also getting smart. It takes time and it takes effort, and these people have so many demands on their time. The cynical thing to say is they’re just busy trying to get elected, but a lot of people in these roles also just have really big other topics that they have to be thinking about. They have to be thinking about wars and healthcare and cost of living and they’re looking at a lot of other stuff from day to day. I saw after ChatGPT, there was a wave in 2023 of, “Oh, maybe Congress is going to get activated on AI, maybe they’re going to actually do something.” It didn’t really turn into anything actually happening, but it did turn into a real moment where a lot of members of Congress and other policymakers started to get smart on AI. It takes some time to learn what a language model is. What even is AI? What is machine learning? They put in some of that work in 2023. I think this year we’re seeing another big wave of interest and people making the time and making the headspace to get smarter on it. I definitely don’t want to say there’s no gap or the government is super smart on AI across the board, but there are some champions who are really smart. I think the staff are generally smarter than people give them credit for. In my mind, it’s much more a question of, “Can the institutions, in the state of functionality that they’re in, get anything significant across the line?” more than, “Are these people just too behind the eight ball?” We’re going to see. There’s a whole bunch of new people. I imagine you have a new cast of characters to go and brief about the technology and what it’s capable of. We’ll see if they have revitalized the institutions. [Laughs] I’m sure it’ll be all fixed overnight. They’re very excited today, but we’ll see how it goes. The other thing that I want to ask you about is the technology itself, the nature of the technology itself, and how you are thinking about it, and the nature of the companies that are making the technology. The reason I’m asking that is I feel like there’s a pretty huge gap in the AI tools and systems most people experience and the way this industry thinks about it. My favorite example of this is we have straight-up asked Anthropic if it thinks Claude is alive and the answer was not no. The answer was a long discursion into the nature of the word “alive.” Well, it depends on what you mean by “alive” to start with. It does. And their answer was, “You need blood.” And I looked at that and I was like, “Who was talking about blood? It wasn’t us. Why are we talking about the requirement of flesh and blood to be alive?” And then some further conversation about the moral status of Claude is yet to be determined. There’s a huge divergence here between the AI overviews most people experience in Google search and “the moral status of Claude is uncertain.” Where are you? How are you situated in that debate? A big part of how I see our role at CSET as an organization, and then also my role as someone who is crossed between these worlds, is trying to translate and voyage to California and then bring back the artifacts and the recountings of my journey. I definitely think that there are a lot of people who have used the free tier of ChatGPT, or they’ve used voice-based models, which generally do worse, or they’ve just used Google AI overviews and they’ve laughed at how stupid Google AI overviews are. They haven’t used agents and they don’t know what frontier models can do. So there is just a basic piece around what the current generation of models can do. There’s a historical piece as well, which I find increasingly relevant as I’m now 10 years into working on AI and national security stuff. If you’re looking at this current moment in time, this snapshot, and saying, “Well, AI seems kind of cool, but it can’t do X,” you have to situate that in the long history of people being like, “Well, AI seems kind of cool, but it can’t do X,” for many, many values of X that have since become totally overcome by events. You can go back and say, “Okay, well, here’s how we were talking about creativity, for example, five or 10 years ago.” Or we were talking about reasoning as this insurmountable thing before you had these new models come out. A huge thing that I am spending time on these days is not just the past and present of AI, but how companies are thinking about what they’re doing, especially the two leading companies, OpenAI and Anthropic, and this is true at Google, Meta, SpaceX to some extent as well. This idea in the Bay Area that it’s just in the water, very normalized of, “Well, first we’re going to figure out how to do recursive self-improvement (RSI) and then we’re going to do that until we have superintelligence that is AI that vastly outstrips humans.” That’s taken for granted in a lot of circles at this point. I think there’s still a ton of alpha in just taking the fact that that is what they’re trying to do and just explaining what that means. It takes a little while to lay out. “What is RSI? Why would you want to do that? What is superintelligence? What does that mean? Is that realistic?” All of that. But it is something I find myself spending a lot of time on these days, and something that there is increasing willingness to take seriously and to listen to in DC as well. Lay that out for me. I think probably a lot of people listening to this show understand what you’re talking about, but we have a big audience. What do you mean by, “We’re going to do RSI and that will lead to superintelligence?” The starting point here is these companies, especially OpenAI and Anthropic, were not set up to be consumer internet companies. A lot of people encountered this whole space after ChatGPT was launched. So the natural slot in their brain that they put a company like OpenAI or Anthropic into is a consumer tech company, where they have an app and I play with their app. I cannot overstate how far that is from the vision of both companies when they started, and also the vision deep in the hearts of some of the top people at both of those companies. The vision deep in their hearts is we’re going to build machines that are as smart as or smarter than people. That is going to be amazing and it’s going to be a huge scientific achievement and it’s going to revolutionize the world and we’re going to be at the forefront of that and we’re going to do everything we possibly can to drive towards that. That’s not a totally brand-new thing. We don’t have to do the whole history of AI, but it started as a field in roughly the 1950s with this idea of whether you can recreate human intelligence inside a machine. That’s kind of the starting point. If we’re talking about people like Sam Altman and Dario Amodei, but also the core people inside, the researchers inside their labs, so your Alec Radfords or your John Schulmans or people like that, that is the vision that got them into this space that is motivating everything that they do. That’s been true since the beginning, since OpenAI was founded in 2015 and Anthropic in 2021. These days, the point that they’re getting to is this idea of RSI, recursive self-improvement, which again, is a very old idea. In the 1960s, this guy called I. J. Good, who worked with Alan Turing, talks about the possibility that you could build an ultra-intelligent machine, meaning a machine that is more intelligent than any human, and then that could build an even more intelligent machine and that could build an even more intelligent machine, which would kick off what he calls an intelligence explosion, meaning that the level of intelligence of the systems is exploding. For decades and decades and decades, this was this theoretical idea of, “Well, if the AI gets smart enough, maybe it can take over building the next generation of AI or directly improving itself.” I think 2025 and 2026, we’ve started to see AI companies saying, “Okay, yeah, this theoretical idea… we’re actually starting to be able to do a minimal version of it in practice.” It’s not handing over all the AI development to the AI, and it’s certainly not saying to GPT-6, like, “Okay, GPT-6, improve yourself.” That’s not what they’re doing. But they are progressively using AI for more and more parts of their overall R&D pipeline, and they are increasingly saying that they’re seeing acceleration from that. They’re seeing their own R&D getting faster and faster. A lot of people elsewhere doubt this, but a lot of people inside the companies really think it. When Demis Hassabis says “we’re in the foothills of the singularity,” this is the kind of thing he means: We might be seeing that initial part of the exponential curve where the AI systems are building the next generation of smarter and smarter systems such that the hockey stick then goes up. At this point, it’s been a part of the culture and a part of the goals for so long that I think people in these companies can lose sight of how totally insane that sounds to many, many people. So I feel like there’s a lot of value in just trying to lay out, “Here’s what they are trying to do. They might not be able to do it, but they might be,” and presenting that to a range of different people. How would you manage that? Demis Hassabis saying “foothills of the singularity” is an all-time quote. I’m not 100 percent sure the people at Google knew he was going to say that on stage to end the conference. Greg Brockman, president of OpenAI, announced a new version of the model a few months ago, and he was like, “Here it is. It’s Astra. It’s AGI now. Have a good time.” And he ended the call. Are you there? Are we at AGI? Is this already here and we just haven’t noticed? I actually wrote something about this. I do not want to say we have AGI. I do want to say we’ve reached the point where I think using AGI as a milestone is just totally unhelpful. The way I put it is the concept of AGI is kind of a fuzzy cloud, which you could think of as different parts of the cloud or different things people mean by AGI. There are people who’ve complained about the term AGI for a long time. Ten years ago it was pretty helpful to be able to say, “Look, the AI systems we have today in 2016, they can all only do one thing and they can recognize speech or they can play Go or whatever, but we’re trying to build this bigger thing that we’re going to call AGI, which is human-level and it’s going to be so general purpose. It’s going to be amazing.” That was a useful term then because this fuzzy cloud of different things AGI might mean was so far away, so you could just point at the fuzzy cloud. But at this point, we’re inside that cloud, meaning we’ve passed some definitions of AGI. A very basic one, for instance, would be even when ChatGPT came out as an artificial general intelligence. ChatGPT was very clearly not a specialist model that was only good at one thing, like recognizing credit card fraud or translation or whatever. It could do many, many, many things. So we’ve reached some definitions of AGI. We’re far from other definitions. Some people will say AGI is when it awakens and is sentient and can do every single thing that any human ever can do. I think we’re pretty far from that. At this point you can have arguments, and people do have arguments, of “well, Astra is AGI,” or “was [OpenAI’s] o3 with tools AGI” or “was ChatGPT AGI,” whatever. OpenAI did this, and Anthropic did this as well. It was kind of an accident that they started doing these consumer products. ChatGPT famously released as a research preview, not as a product. But it was so successful that these research labs that wanted to be doing research, that wanted to be focusing on the big ideas and on building the most event systems, had this accidental massive commercial success at the same time as they were realizing that they were going to need an enormous amount of capital to scale. The best research approaches that they could do didn’t involve being really smart and thoughtful and having great ideas. They involved having gigantic computing clusters that cost, at this point, hundreds of billions of dollars. This is a long way of saying, yes, I agree with you, they’ve become businesses, but I think it is not because they’ve gone through some mindset shift. I think it’s because the path of the tech tree that we’re going down both requires enormous amounts of capital and also is capable of generating enormous amounts of revenue because it is actually useful along the way. You see this in the fact that both OpenAI and Anthropic have gone this route, even though their management philosophies and research philosophies are quite different, that it’s an imperative that they both had to make the money and it was so easy for them to build enormously revenue-generating businesses because the tech was so useful long before it reached the point of machine god. So I think that’s a long way of agreeing with you, but with some extra color maybe. Yeah, I mean, Kevin would tell you that he could have retitled that book, “Fuck This Guy: A Story of AI CEOs.” They don’t like each other. If you had to relive that moment [of the OpenAI board vote] and say, “I don’t trust Sam,” would you relive that moment? Would you do it the same way? Oh, for sure. I mean, we went into it knowing that it was going to suck. So yeah, for sure. Do you think that these guys are trustworthy? Do you think Sam is trustworthy? I think my stance on that is pretty clear, and I also think that if our hopes for the future are pinned on any one individual being trustworthy, then we’re pretty screwed. That’s why I do the work that I do, because I think we need to have different structures and many more people involved with many more perspectives being represented. You have some hindsight now. You knew it was going to suck going into it. You definitely know it sucked coming out of it. What would you have done differently about that time? It’s kind of hard to give the full answer to that because it would take unpicking all this stuff and all these legal restrictions and blah, blah, blah, blah. For sure a thing would have been building stronger relationships with executives on the team. The way that the company related to the board could have been different if more board members had had that. I knew some of the folks pretty well, but that’s one thing. I don’t know. I think we could have… Yeah, no, I think beyond that, it just gets hard to… You have to go in and say, “What were all the different micro decisions and why do we make those decisions and which ones could be—” What is the show? It’s a show about decisions. I’ve got another hour. [Laughs] Yeah, yeah, yeah. No, and then my answers would all get annoying and legal. Fair enough. I’m curious about it because as they go public, there will be market forces acting on them in a totally new way. There will be an investor class. There’ll be an entire CNBC machine that wakes up every day and is like, “Is Anthropic winning or is OpenAI winning?” That is a race dynamic that might be really healthy. It might keep them from trying to kill everyone in the world because they have a bunch of investors looking for their next quarterly earnings, or it might push them further into an unhealthy kind of race. How do you see that playing out, given what you know of these people? It’s going to be really interesting to see if going public is good or bad for their governance. A lot of people are like, “Oh no, going public, there’s going to be so much pressure to make a profit that they’re not going to be able to consider other things.” But at the same time, the corporate governance of public companies is much more structured, much more regulated, and subject to much more external scrutiny than for private companies. I think even things like getting to see Anthropic’s S-1 and thinking, “Okay, what are they doing and why are they doing it? And how do they think about the risks they’re facing, and how do they communicate about those with investors?” Or even things like the Trump administration putting in place this kind of accord, they call it “Super Intelligence,” that several of the leading companies signed. That was structured around, for example, having certain types of things being reported to an independent committee of the board. That idea of an independent committee of the board is kind of toothless if it’s a private company that is deciding on its own. I thought about you when I read that. I was like, “Boy, some independent boards have gotten in a lot of trouble before.” But if it’s a public company, then an independent committee of the board has a pretty strong legal meaning. So I don’t know. It’s something that I’m watching with great interest. The other race dynamic here is China. You mentioned China before. Inside of our country, a bunch of labs are going to go public. They’re going to become some of the richest companies in the history of the world, and they’re going to fight for every dollar that capitalism can generate, and hopefully that restrains them. The market forces will restrain them, and hopefully your work with legislators in this country does something. And then there’s a whole other country that doesn’t listen to us or have anything to do with us, and they’re just going to distill our models and do whatever they want. That is the other argument for not placing any restrictions on these companies that everyone hears all the time. What should I make of that? I’m of two minds about it. How should I think about it? Yeah. I think of this as the ”But China!” argument, which is like, “Well, yeah, we should do this, we should do that, ‘But China!’” I think the way to engage with it is an actual genuine problem that we have to grapple with, and we should be strategic and thoughtful about it and do our best to try and solve it as a problem as opposed to using it as a throwaway excuse. Like, “Oh yeah, sure, sure, sure. All that stuff would be so nice, ‘But China!’, so we’re stuck. There’s nothing we can do.” So what does that look like in practice? If you’re serious about wanting the US to have stronger AI than China, then you need to think really hard about how much US AI development is helping Chinese AI progress. So the one that people talk about all the time, as you mentioned, is distillation, which is, “Are they using US models to generate massive amounts of training data for their own models and therefore progressing faster than they would otherwise?” So certainly I think it makes sense to try and crack down on that and prevent it from happening. But another one, for example, is security and how easy would it be for Chinese actors or other actors, frankly, to steal algorithmic secrets, to steal wholesale model weights. If they can steal the weights of your Astra or your Mythos model and just take them back to their own servers, your lead has vanished. You now have a lead of zero. Right now these companies, especially the smaller ones, but even OpenAI and Anthropic, do not have very good security. We’ve seen both of them over the last few months have external teams manage to hack into spaces that have large amounts of algorithmic secrets. In OpenAI’s case, it was their monorepo and GitHub, which had all of their code. And in Anthropic’s case, I think — and actually maybe the OpenAI case also involved this — the hackers got access to Slack. You’re just going to have so insanely much rich information about how to build better AI if you can get that access. So when our AI gets better, are we actually lengthening our lead or are we just pulling China along with us in these different ways? The other aspect of this is just seriously treating China as an actor in this space and trying to think seriously about their motivations and their likely actions and responses. In my mind, a huge reason that a lot of things are not happening right now is most people are not convinced about this threat model that AI will become the machine god and will take over and humans will all die or will be subservient or whatever. I think it’s fair for people to not be convinced of that, because the evidence is sort of conflicting and unclear, but if that is actually what we think could seriously happen, then China doesn’t want that either. So then it becomes a question of, “Okay, how do we try and get them on the same page of, ‘this threat that we’re worried about is a real threat to worry about?’ Because then they will be making their own decisions in their own self-interest.” I think an approach of, “Well, the US has to force China to do something using some kind of leverage,” is never ever going to work. But an approach of, “Well, look, if we think this is a serious problem that’s going to affect us as humans, and the people in China are also humans, and also if we think this is a problem around who has control, the Chinese Communist Party really, really wants to have control, and so they’re going to have their own incentives and their own decision-making around how to fix that.” Well, let me put it on a spectrum for you. This is very dumb and you’re going to laugh, but just go with me on this. On the one end, it is nuclear weapons and the Chinese government wants a nuclear weapon and they’re going to do whatever they can to control that weapon and they will run their industries differently. If they get out of line, the CEO of Alibaba goes. He just disappears for a while and then comes back — Chinese government stuff. We need a nuclear weapon, too. If we don’t get there first, then we’ll never get the nonproliferation treaty that we need to keep us all safe for mutually assured destruction. That’s one framework. Way on the other end, I spent five years of my life listening to telecom executives tell me that if we didn’t build 5G networks first, China would get them, and then something. No one could ever tell me what the “something” was. Where on that spectrum between 5G and nuclear weapons is the US-China AI race? I think we need another dimension because in that example, your dimension is significance. But I think the controllability is a huge question as well. So it’s like, what are the examples that people use? Is it a nuclear weapon or is it dragons from House of the Dragon? Casey Newton had a great Platformer post where he explained he was watching House of the Dragon and thought, “This is what the AI companies are doing. They’re trying to build these things that they think will help them, but actually it’s just going to rain down destruction.” [Laughs] Casey told me he was buying an iPhone Duo so he could watch more TV. He’s a dear friend, but okay. But I think that’s really important because if we think this is a technology we can control, then obviously we want to have the best technology. Obviously, we want to go foot to the floor, get there as fast as we can, and the same is true for China. The question is, if we are not sure if we can control it, then what do we do? Maybe we want to be more cautious and then maybe we want to try and figure out a way to not have China just be overtaking us. But if we’re correct we should be worried about— So that’s nuclear weapons. Well, no, but if it’s dragons, if we’re correct that we need to be worried about whether we can control this, then that’s also something that should be interesting to China. I remember this Casey post, but let me just try to pull this apart so I understand it. The difference between dragons and nuclear weapons is the dragons have some agency, right? They can go away and do bad things on their own. Yes. The dragons might just decide to burn down your whole city. Obviously these are machines — they’re just math, they’re not magical. So instead of dragons, you could think of it as nuclear weapons with faulty control settings, where you build nuclear weapons, but it’s impossible to be sure that it’s not just going to go off and fly to a city and fly to one of your own cities and wipe you out. That’s a very different technology than real nuclear weapons that exist. It is true. No one ever said that about 5G. I’ll be clear about that. The reason I’m asking about this is because those problems do align nation-states, right? We do have nuclear nonproliferation agreements. As you mentioned, there are all kinds of incentives for nation-states to not do cyberattacks willy-nilly because those have real-world consequences. Is there any evidence that these governments have started to align on these problems? Or is it still the pure “But China!” race dynamic? I actually think there is starting to be some early evidence. One way I think about what happened this year in AI from a policy perspective, less than a product or economic perspective, is we saw these two big demonstrations of the two major concerns people have. So the two major concerns are misuse and misalignment, meaning misuse is bad people using AI for bad things and misalignment is AI going rogue or doing things we didn’t want. So this year we had Mythos and we had the Hugging Face attack. Both of those are just really vivid, crisp real-world demonstrations of what these misuse and misalignment concerns could look like. The US and Chinese governments are starting from very different places on AI regulation. They’re both starting from where they started, and what they did with, internet regulation. So the US is starting from a “hands off, laissez-faire, absolutely nothing, do whatever you want” approach. China is starting from a massively locked-down internet with tons of censorship and the Great Firewall. So those are two very different starting points. I’m not a China expert, but I operate a lot in China circles and I’ve lived in China and so on. But it seems like just over the past even one to three months, starting from those two very different points, they are seeing more in common around threats from major cyberattacks and also threats of loss of control. I’m a language nerd and it’s really interesting tracking the different language China uses about AI. So they’re now talking about loss of control as a thing, but they probably usually don’t mean the same thing that Westerners mean where “loss of control” is like “AI takeover.” They probably mean something more prosaic, but then sometimes they talk about “extreme loss of control,” which maybe is the thing we mean. I do think that there are starting to be some signs of convergence. I think it’ll be a long road. The state of the US-China relationship is such that there’s going to be very, very, very little trust on either side. So I am not optimistic that they’ll just get to sit down in a room and hash out a deal and everything will be great. But I think there is enough space. Basically, if there’s enough shared threat perception, then it might be possible at some point in the future to do something about that. Helen, you’ve given me so much time. As you can tell, I’m just delighted with this conversation. It’s been very fun. We are on the cusp of a new Congress. There are a bunch of new governors. The data center referendums passed overwhelmingly in this country. There’s a new set of regulators in town, right? They’re going to do some stuff. What are some signs people should look for to indicate we’re going to be on the right path and what are some signs that we’re just chasing our tail? Set AI aside, forget about AI. Congress in general is very bad at passing things right now. This is not a this administration thing, this is not an AI thing. So one sign is like, can Congress pass anything? That will be a good sign. It’s also really interesting to look at what state legislatures have been doing in AI. There’s been a lot of concern about the possibility of a state patchwork on AI, with different states passing conflicting things. With the issues that we’ve been talking about today, which I think of as frontier AI risks or the risks from the most advanced systems, there’s actually been a pretty coordinated push in different states. California passed this one bill and then New York passed almost the same bill with just a little more added to it. And then Illinois passed almost the same bill with a little more added to it. I think there’s going to be a lot of momentum over the next year or two to keep building on that at the state level. So that is something that I’ll be watching. Even just specifically California is already looking at how they can strengthen things. So that is something I’ll be looking for. I think honestly, with such a Democratic Congress, I am also concerned that they will overstep here, that they will try and do something that is too sweeping. You had this huge mess in Colorado where they passed this giant AI bill that then was a terrible idea. And so then they had all these committees and follow-up and it was awful. A lot of what we need right now is focused on these frontier systems and the possibility that we have really, really advanced systems in a short amount of time and having much more transparency around that and much clearer standards for how they manage risk. I would not be that excited about an attempt to do a really comprehensive AI regulatory push that covers AI all across the economy and all different kinds of AI systems that are less advanced. There are negative signals that are like “nothing’s going to happen,” and there are negative signals like, “oh, maybe too much is going to happen,” but it’ll be interesting to see where they get to. I suspect we’re going to want to have you back as this Congress starts to get to work and we see some of these ideas. I would love to. I’m eager for your take on it. Thank you so much for being on Decoder. Thanks so much. This was really fun. Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email!

articles.title: 北 김정은 최측근 조용원, APEC 앞두고 러시아 방문
articles.snippet: 김정은 북한 노동당 총비서의 최측근인 조용원 노동당 조직비서 겸 조직지도부장이 러시아를 방문했다. 오는 18일 중국 선전에서 열리는 아시아태평양경제협력체(APEC) 정상회의에서 미국과 중국, 러시아의 정상 회동을 앞두고 북러 양측의 고위급 협의가 진행되는 것이다.노동당 기관지 노동신문은 15일 조 비서를 대표로 하는 북한의 당·정부 대표단이 러시아를 방문하기 위해 14일 평양을 떠나 모스크바에 도착했다고 보도했다.신문에 따르면 이번 방문은 러시아 집권 여당인 통합러시아당 드미트리 메드베데프 대표의 초청에 따라 이뤄졌다.이날 평양국제공항에는 최선희 외무상, 김성남 노동당 국제비서 등 북한의 대외정책을 담당하는 핵심 간부들과 안드레이 레오니도비치 포드욜리셰프 주북 러시아대사 등이 나와 대표단을 전송했다.모스크바에서는 안드레이 클리모프 통합러시아당 최고이사회 뷰로(정치국) 및 관계자와 신홍철 주러시아 북한대사 및 대사관 관계자들이 대표단을 맞이했다.이번 북한 당·정부 대표단의 방

articles.title: 북한 국기 디자인 1948년 이후 처음 변경
articles.snippet: 북한이 1948년 건국 이후 처음으로 국기의 가로세로 비율을 변경했다고 미국의 북한 전문 매체 NK 뉴스(NK NEWS)가 13일(현지시각) 보도했다. 김일성 초대 지도자와 밀접하게 연관된 수십 년 된 국기 디자인과 결별한 것이다.북한 당국의 공식 웹사이트인 내나라가 최근 기존의 가로 세로 비율 1:2를 적용한 국기 대신 1:1.65 비율의 국기를 게시하기 시작했다.국기 양쪽 위아래에 있는 두 개의 가느다란 흰색 줄무늬도 이전보다 두꺼워진 것으로 보인다. 폭이 위아래 파란색 줄무늬 폭의 약 3분의 1 수준으로 넓어졌다.내나라에 게시된 국기 변경은 북한의 형식적인 의회가 승인한 헌법 개정 이후인 지난달 17일부터 11월10일 사이 어느 시점에 이뤄진 것으로 보인다.이 변경은 개정 사회주의헌법 제7장 제166조에 따라 2026년 3월23일 공식 비준됐다. 그러나 북한 측 자료를 통해 변경 사실이 확인된 것은 내나라가 지난 10일 새 헌법 전문을 게시한 이후였다.북한 관영 매체

articles.snippet: 미국에서 광복군을 후원한 호시한 지사(1885∼1956)와 러시아 연해주에서 독립운동을 하다 우즈베키스탄으로 강제 이주당한 이괄 지사(1898∼1963)의 유해가 고국으로 돌아온다. 우즈베키스탄에 안장된 독립유공자의 유해가 국내로 봉환되는 것은 이번이 처음이다.국가보훈부는 제87회 순국선열의 날(17일)을 앞두고 두 지사와 배우자들의 유해를 15일 인천국제공항을 통해 봉환한다고 13일 밝혔다. 권오을 보훈부 장관이 공항에서 유해를 직접 영접할 계획이다. 유해 봉환식은 16일 서울 서대문독립공원 3·1독립선언기념탑에서 열린다. 보훈부는 호 지사가 서대문형무소에 수감됐던 이력을 고려했다고 설명했다. 두 지사의 유해는 이후 국립대전현충원에 안장된다.서울 교남동 출신인 호 지사는 1914년 미국에서 한인소년병학교 운영을 지원하는 단체를 조직했고, 3·1운동 직후인 1919년 5월 국내에서 군자금 모금을 계획하다 일제에 체포됐다. 이후 중국 상하이를 거쳐 미국으로 돌아가 중국항일전쟁 동정

articles.title: 호시한-이괄 지사 유해 돌아온다… 우즈베키스탄서 첫 봉환
articles.snippet: 미국에서 광복군을 후원한 호시한 지사(1885∼1956)와 러시아 연해주에서 독립운동을 하다 우즈베키스탄으로 강제 이주당한 이괄 지사(1898∼1963)의 유해가 고국으로 돌아온다. 우즈베키스탄에 안장된 독립유공자의 유해가 국내로 봉환되는 것은 이번이 처음이다.국가보훈부는 제87회 순국선열의 날(17일)을 앞두고 두 지사와 배우자들의 유해를 15일 인천국제공항을 통해 봉환한다고 13일 밝혔다. 권오을 보훈부 장관이 공항에서 유해를 직접 영접할 계획이다. 유해 봉환식은 16일 서울 서대문독립공원 3·1독립선언기념탑에서 열린다. 보훈부는 호 지사가 서대문형무소에 수감됐던 이력을 고려했다고 설명했다. 두 지사의 유해는 이후 국립대전현충원에 안장된다.서울 교남동 출신인 호 지사는 1914년 미국에서 한인소년병학교 운영을 지원하는 단체를 조직했고, 3·1운동 직후인 1919년 5월 국내에서 군자금 모금을 계획하다 일제에 체포됐다. 이후 중국 상하이를 거쳐 미국으로 돌아가 중국항일전쟁 동정

articles.title: 조현 “중국이 APEC에 北 초청할 가능성, 크지 않아”
articles.snippet: 조현 외교부 장관은 다음 주 중국 선전에서 열리는 아시아태평양경제협력체(APEC)에 북한이 등장할 가능성은 크지 않다고 13일 밝혔다. 조 장관은 이날 오전 한중외교장관회담을 위해 중국으로 출국하기 전 김포국제공항에서 취재진과 만나 중국의 북미회담 중재 의지가 있는지를 묻는 질문에 “있지만 적극적으로 이번 APEC에 초청해서 할 것이냐, 그런 것은 별로 크진 않은 것 같다”라고 말했다. 이날 중국에서 열릴 한중외교장관회담의 주된 의제에 대해선 “한중 관계 전반, 특히 이제 APEC 회담을 앞두고 한중 간 조율해야 될 일, 북한과의 문제, 특히 북미회담 가능성도 있기 때문에 중국과 포괄적으로 논의할 예정”이라고 말했다.조 장관은 이날부터 14일까지 중국을 찾아 중국 왕이 외교부장과 회담 및 만찬을 갖는다. 이번 회담은 지난 8월 왕 부장 방한 이후 3개월 만이다. 양국 외교 수장은 회담에서 한중 관계와 한반도를 비롯한 지역 정세를 논의할 것으로 예상된다. 특히 최근 왕 부장이

articles.snippet: 이재명 대통령이 13일 주가 상승을 의미하는 빨간 넥타이를 매고 한국거래소를 찾아 “산이 높으면 골이 깊지만, 반대로 골이 깊으면 산이 높지 않을까 생각한다”며 최근 조정 중인 증시의 반등에 대한 기대감을 나타냈다. 이날 서울 영등포구 여의도 거래소에서 ‘자본시장 정책 간담회’를 주재한 이 대통령은 “자본시장 정상화는 우리 정부의 확고한 정책 방향이고 의지”라고 강조했다. 이 대통령이 거래소를 찾은 건 취임 후 첫 외부 일정이었던 지난해 6월 11일 이후 두 번째다. 이 대통령은 “대한민국 주식시장에 상장돼 있다는 이유로 똑같은 주식이 저평가받는 것은 매우 불합리한 비정상”이라며 “비정상을 정상화하는 것이 우리 정부의 핵심 과제”라고 밝혔다. 그러면서 “시장 정상화의 가장 큰 장치가 적대적 인수합병(M&A)”이라며 적대적 M&A를 막는 장치에 대한 전수조사를 주문했다. 이 대통령은 자본시장 개혁을 전담할 고위급 기구 구성도 지시했다. 이날 간담회에는 이형일 경제부

articles.title: 조희대 탄핵 다시 꺼내드는 민주당
articles.snippet: 더불어민주당에서 조희대 대법원장 탄핵론이 재점화되고 있다. 조 대법원장 국정조사 추진을 보류했던 당 지도부가 20일 한덕수 전 국무총리 구속 만료를 앞두고 강경 대응을 검토하고 나선 것. 당내 강경파가 연일 탄핵을 촉구하며 지도부를 압박한 것도 영향을 미쳤다는 분석이 나온다. 민주당 김민석 대표는 13일 최고위원회의에서 “한덕수 석방은 내란 부활을 상징하는 국민적 금기선”이라며 “조희대 사법부에 경고한다. 넘지 말아야 할 선이 있다”고 말했다. 이어 “금기선을 넘으면 그 이후 모든 상황에 대한 책임을 져야 할 것”이라고 강조했다. 내란 중요임무종사 혐의로 2심에서 징역 15년을 선고받은 한 전 총리는 20일 0시 상고심 구속 기간이 만료된다. 대법원 전원합의체는 구속 기간 만료 하루 전인 19일 두 번째 심리를 열기로 했다. 대법원은 20일 전 선고 여부를 이르면 16일 공지할 예정이다. 이에 따라 민주당의 대응도 탄핵으로 무게중심이 옮겨갈 가능성이 거론된다. 김 대표는 당초 조

articles.title: 조희대 탄핵 다시 꺼내드는 민주당
articles.snippet: 더불어민주당에서 조희대 대법원장 탄핵론이 재점화되고 있다. 조 대법원장 국정조사 추진을 보류했던 당 지도부가 20일 한덕수 전 국무총리 구속 만료를 앞두고 강경 대응을 검토하고 나선 것. 당내 강경파가 연일 탄핵을 촉구하며 지도부를 압박한 것도 영향을 미쳤다는 분석이 나온다. 민주당 김민석 대표는 13일 최고위원회의에서 “한덕수 석방은 내란 부활을 상징하는 국민적 금기선”이라며 “조희대 사법부에 경고한다. 넘지 말아야 할 선이 있다”고 말했다. 이어 “금기선을 넘으면 그 이후 모든 상황에 대한 책임을 져야 할 것”이라고 강조했다. 내란 중요임무종사 혐의로 2심에서 징역 15년을 선고받은 한 전 총리는 20일 0시 상고심 구속 기간이 만료된다. 대법원 전원합의체는 구속 기간 만료 하루 전인 19일 두 번째 심리를 열기로 했다. 대법원은 20일 전 선고 여부를 이르면 16일 공지할 예정이다. 이에 따라 민주당의 대응도 탄핵으로 무게중심이 옮겨갈 가능성이 거론된다. 김 대표는 당초 조

articles.title: 경찰, ‘부정청약’ 이혜훈 80억 반포 원펜타스 몰수 신청
articles.snippet: 시세 약 80억 원대 서울 서초구 반포동 아파트를 부정한 방법으로 분양받았다는 의혹을 받는 이혜훈 전 기획예산처 장관 후보자가 공소청에 넘겨졌다. 경찰은 이 전 후보자가 장남을 부양가족에 포함해 청약 가점을 부풀렸으며, 이로 인해 당첨 여부가 달라졌다고 판단했다. 서울경찰청 광역수사단 금융범죄수사대는 13일 이 전 후보자를 사기, 업무방해, 주민등록법 위반 혐의로 불구속 송치했다고 밝혔다. 시민단체 등의 첫 고발장이 접수된 지 10개월 만이다. 이 전 후보자는 결혼식을 올리고 혼인신고를 하지 않은 장남을 미혼 부양가족으로 신고해 청약 가점을 높이는 방식으로 2024년 ‘래미안 원펜타스’ 청약에 당첨된 혐의를 받는다. 이 전 후보자는 기획예산처 장관 후보자 인사청문회에서 장남 부부의 관계가 나빠져 혼인신고가 늦어졌다는 취지로 해명했다. 그러나 경찰은 장남이 부양가족에서 빠졌다면 가점이 낮아져 당첨이 어려웠을 것으로 판단했다. 경찰은 해당 아파트에 대해 기소 전 몰수보전을 신청하고,

articles.title: 北 김정은 최측근 조용원, APEC 앞두고 러시아 방문
articles.snippet: 김정은 북한 노동당 총비서의 최측근인 조용원 노동당 조직비서 겸 조직지도부장이 러시아를 방문했다. 오는 18일 중국 선전에서 열리는 아시아태평양경제협력체(APEC) 정상회의에서 미국과 중국, 러시아의 정상 회동을 앞두고 북러 양측의 고위급 협의가 진행되는 것이다.노동당 기관지 노동신문은 15일 조 비서를 대표로 하는 북한의 당·정부 대표단이 러시아를 방문하기 위해 14일 평양을 떠나 모스크바에 도착했다고 보도했다.신문에 따르면 이번 방문은 러시아 집권 여당인 통합러시아당 드미트리 메드베데프 대표의 초청에 따라 이뤄졌다.이날 평양국제공항에는 최선희 외무상, 김성남 노동당 국제비서 등 북한의 대외정책을 담당하는 핵심 간부들과 안드레이 레오니도비치 포드욜리셰프 주북 러시아대사 등이 나와 대표단을 전송했다.모스크바에서는 안드레이 클리모프 통합러시아당 최고이사회 뷰로(정치국) 및 관계자와 신홍철 주러시아 북한대사 및 대사관 관계자들이 대표단을 맞이했다.이번 북한 당·정부 대표단의 방

articles.title: 눈보라에 백두산 오르는 北여성들…“가면 애국, 안 가면 변절”[주성하의 ‘北토크’]

articles.title: If you’re wondering what a Reform government might look like, just look at its chaotic record in Wales | Will Hayward
articles.snippet: As the main opposition in the Senedd, the party should be taking politics seriously. Spoiler alert: it’s not In May 2026, Reform UK became the official opposition inside the Welsh Senedd. It was the best result the party had ever received in a national parliament – and since that time it has been a wild ride. Given that its leader, Nigel Farage, claims he expects to one day lead the UK government, how it performs in Wales matters more than just for the people of Cymru; it gives the rest of the UK a sense of what it could expect if Reform does well in the next general election. Just to give you a taste, here are two developments. In September, Reform’s leader in Wales, Dan Thomas, resigned after he was arrested and released on bail on suspicion of assault and coercive or controlling behaviour. (Thomas said that he had done “nothing wrong” but resigned to avoid becoming a “distraction”.) It has also lost one of its members in a bizarre defection from the rightwing Reform (which has been sceptical about even the existence of the Welsh parliament) to the leftwing Plaid Cymru (which wants more devolution and ultimately an independent Wales). Will Hayward is a Guardian columnist. He publishes a regular newsletter on Welsh politics Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘It was a train wreck! I was terrified’: how the new James Bond will be announced – and what can go wrong
articles.snippet: As Amazon MGM Studios prepares to announce the next 007, much rides on how the news is broken. From double bookings to health and safety embarrassments, we look back at how not to do it And then there were five. While nothing has been officially announced, it is widely understood that the shortlist to replace Daniel Craig as James Bond is now down to a handful of actors: Callum Turner, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor, Robert Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult. The hunt for a new Bond comes at a propitious moment for the franchise as a whole, 25 films in (not counting the two “unofficial” entries, Casino Royale in 1967 and Never Say Never Again in 1983). After Daniel Craig stood down from the role after completing No Time to Die (in which Bond appeared to be killed in a missile strike), Amazon MGM Studios paid over $1bn to acquire “creative control” from Barbara Broccoli and Michael G Wilson, the British-American heirs to the series’ original producer Albert “Cubby” Broccoli and longtime stewards of the Bond films. articles.title: Very good boys? The dark, dystopian rise of robot dogs | Arwa Mahwadi
articles.snippet: Pups that carry your shopping are one thing – but what about the mechanical canines being bought up in the US by ICE? Or the mutant mutts due to be developed by a startup called Warhound? Have you ever wanted to hang out with a dog with no fur, no face and a chip in its shoulder? If so, I suggest you head to San Francisco, where a startup called Dimensional has been paying people $20 (£15) an hour to walk four-legged robot dogs. This isn’t because the dogs need the exercise – it is because the company needs the training data. As reported in the New York Times, the goal is to develop “operating systems that can integrate with AI agents so the machines can act more independently”. What exactly will these machines do when they can act more independently? The founder of Dimensional insists they will help people. They might carry groceries home, for example, which is certainly something my tiny chihuahua-mix is incapable of. Continue reading...
